title: The page
hookLine: Mishnah and Gemara in the center, Rashi on the inner margin, Tosafot on the outer

cards: Hold a printed page of Talmud at arm's length, and before you read a single word, you see a shape. A block of large letters in the middle.
Columns of smaller print wrapping around it on both sides, like hands cupping something. Notes squeezed into the edges.
It looks less like a page of a book and more like a map of a city, with a town square in the center and streets leading out. That shape isn't decoration. Every block on it is somebody talking.

teach.b: The page. In the standard printed Talmud, the pages share one basic layout, and once you know it, you can find your way around a tractate. First, the center.
That large block holds the Mishnah and the Gemara: the case, the voices, and the long conversation of the past week. It's the town square. Everything else on the page points back to it.
Second, the inner margin, the column nearest the binding. That's Rashi, the explainer, walking alongside the text word by word, telling you what a phrase means and how the argument moves.
If you're lost, look to the inside.
Third, the outer margin, the column nearest the edge. That's Tosafot, a circle of later scholars who ask hard questions: of the Gemara, of other pages, and sometimes of Rashi himself.
So the explainer and his questioners sit on either side of the text, facing each other across it. Fourth, the edges.
Around and below, in still smaller print, are notes that send you elsewhere: to a verse, to a law code, to a parallel discussion on another page.
These voices lived in different places and times, and none of them could hear the others in life.
The printed page puts them within arm's reach of each other. A student who opens it steps into the middle.

how: Students of the Talmud learn the page's layout early: they read the Mishnah and Gemara in the center, turn to Rashi on the inner margin for explanation, and to Tosafot on the outer margin for questions and cross-references.

games.q: you've opened a page of Talmud. there's an Aramaic phrase in the center block you can't make sense of. where do you look first?
o: the notes at the bottom edge.
games.why: the inner margin, nearest the binding: that's Rashi, explaining the text word by word. the outer margin is where Tosafot ask their questions.

practice: Close your eyes and build the page: the block in the center, Rashi on the inside near the spine, Tosafot on the outside near the edge, little notes along the borders.
Now put yourself on it: would your voice ask, explain, or send someone elsewhere? Breathe there for a while, a small voice in a very old margin.

wordCard.voice: The page. Mishnah and Gemara in the center, Rashi on the inner margin, Tosafot on the outer, notes at the edges: one page, many voices. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: daf, the word learners use for a page of Talmud.

carryVoice: Your line: the page is a conversation. Voices who never met, sharing one sheet of paper. See you tomorrow.
